title: Strain-induced disorder from Schottky gates on high mobility 2DEGs
authors: Sambit Mohapatra, Lukas Berg, Jean-Baptiste Cuvellier, Yan Sun, Abdelhanin Aassime, Alan Durnez, Antonella Cavanna, Dominique Mailly, Ulf Gennser
abstract: Electrostatic gates on two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) in GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures are essential for numerous studies of correlation driven phenomena, many performed within the fractional quantum Hall effect. However, the most commonly used type of gates, the metallic Schottky gate, has the propensity to adversely impact the electron mobility and suppress the fractional quantum Hall states. Here we demonstrate through commensurability oscillations under specially designed nanostructured superlattice gates, that strain effects are responsible for the mobility reduction. The experimental results agree well with COMSOL Multiphysics simulations. In a regular, unpatterned gate the disordered, granular nature of the metal film fills the same role as the superlattice in creating a strain field penetrating down to the 2DEG, as we show with a simplified model. These results will help in understanding, improving and finding novel methods to reduce strain-induced disorder in gated high-mobility 2DEGs.
summary: This paper demonstrates that metallic gates degrade the performance of high-mobility 2DEGs by inducing strain. By analyzing commensurability oscillations, the authors prove that this disorder originates from strain fields, which are modeled using detailed simulations incorporating the piezoelectric effect. The findings offer a pathway to designing gates that minimize detrimental strain effects.
main_problem: The study investigates how strain induced by metallic Schottky gates degrades electron mobility and suppresses correlated quantum Hall states in high-mobility 2DEGs.
main_result: The mobility reduction and the observation of commensurability oscillations (COs) are successfully attributed to strain fields generated by the patterned gates, which are confirmed by detailed simulations.
method: The research combines low-temperature magnetoresistance measurements (observing COs) with advanced finite-element simulations (COMSOL Multiphysics) to model strain propagation and its coupling to the 2DEG potential via the piezoelectric effect.
model_or_system: The physical system is a 2DEG in GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures patterned with metallic superlattices. The model incorporates strain mechanics, the piezoelectric effect, and quantum transport theory (manifested through COs).
key_observables: Electron mobility ($\mu$), commensurability oscillations ($ho_{xx}(B)$), and the strain tensor components ($S_{xx}, S_{yy}, S_{xy}$).
important_parameters: Gate periodicity ($P$), metal thickness, 2DEG depth ($D$), and temperature ($T$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that strain is the dominant source of disorder; the analysis relies on the first-order piezoelectric approximation and simplified boundary conditions in simulations.
figures_summary: Figures compare mobility vs. density for different gate thicknesses, show COs in patterned vs. unpatterned gates, and map simulated strain components ($S_{xy}$) and potential modulation ($V_0$) dependence on gate geometry and depth.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from initial observations of mobility degradation with uniform gates to using patterned gates to induce measurable COs. It then quantitatively links the CO amplitude to simulated strain fields, confirming the role of piezoelectricity and developing guidelines for gate design.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, experimentally verifiable mechanism (strain coupling) for disorder in highly tunable quantum systems, which is crucial for engineering quantum devices where material interfaces and strain control are paramount.
